Cross-cutting observations for Batch E [Claude reading]: Relating to God engages the whole inner seat, and the texts say so by formula.; "With all your heart and with all your soul" governs: serving (Deu 10:12; Jos 22:5); keeping the law and renewing the covenant (2Ki 23:3; 2Ch 34:31; Deu 30:10); loving after circumcision of heart (Deu 30:6); praying and returning (1Ki 8:48); being tested (Deu 13:3); "With my whole heart" governs thanks, praise, crying and seeking.; The formula also appears of God (Jer 32:41).; The heart is where the relation to God is located, examined and known.; It prays without voice (1Sa 1:13) and cries (Lam 2:18).; It holds the law (Psa 37:31) and trusts (Psa 28:7).; It believes (Rom 10:10) and is circumcised (Deu 30:6).; It is the organ God tests (§8.1). Knowing hearts is the ground of God's forgiveness (1Ki 8:39) and of his giving the Spirit (Act 15:8).; Where heart and lips diverge, the lips do not count (Hos 7:14; Isa 29:13).; The soul is the self in address. It is spoken to by its owner ("Bless the Lord, O my soul"; "Why are you cast down, O my soul"), and asked to be spoken to by God ("Say to my soul, 'I am your salvation'", Psa 35:3). It is also the life that is: asked for (Est 7:3; 1Ki 17:21); asked to die (1Ki 19:4; Jon 4:8); redeemed, ransomed and atoned for (§9.1, §11.1); delivered or lost (§11.3); The human spirit is most active in this batch.; It prays and sings apart from the mind (1Co 14:14–16).; It serves (Rom 1:9) and worships in spirit (Joh 4:23–24).; It rejoices in the Savior (Luk 1:47) and is renewed (Eze 36:26; Eph 4:23).; It receives the benediction "grace be with your spirit".; At death it is the part committed to God (Psa 31:5; Luk 23:46; Act 7:59; Mat 27:50).; Its complaint voices anguish (Job 7:11), and its brokenness blocks hearing (Exo 6:9).; The divine Spirit relates to God on the person's behalf.; It cries "Abba" in the heart (Gal 4:6) and intercedes within the searched heart (Rom 8:26–27).; It bears witness (Heb 10:15) and writes on hearts (2Co 3:3).; It circumcises the heart (Rom 2:29) and renews (Tit 3:5).; It gives faith and gifts (1Co 12:9; Gal 3:2) and speaks through the prophet (2Sa 23:2).; It can itself be tested (Act 5:9), resisted (Act 7:51) and outraged (Heb 10:29).; Other spirits relate to God too, and are judged by that relation.

3.2 Totality and wholeness formulas: *Heart and soul (and might):*; "with all your heart and with all your soul (and with all your might)" (Deu 4:29; 6:5; 10:12; 11:13; 13:3; 26:16; 30:2, 6, 10; Jos 22:5; 1Ki 2:4; 8:48; 2Ki 23:3, 25; 2Ch 6:38; 15:12; 34:31; Jer 32:41 — said of God); "you know in your hearts and souls" (Jos 23:14); "lay up these words … in your heart and in your soul" (Deu 11:18); "keep your soul diligently, lest … they depart from your heart" (Deu 4:9); "I am with you heart and soul" (1Sa 14:7, ESV idiom; only *lēvāv* is tagged); "one heart and soul" (Act 4:32); *NT expansion — heart, soul, mind, strength:* Mat 22:37; Mar 12:30; Luk 10:27; "heart … understanding … strength" (Mar 12:33).; *Whole person with an outer term added:*; "spirit and soul and body" (1Th 5:23); "soul and body" (Isa 10:18; Mat 10:28; Psa 31:9; Pro 16:24); "heart and flesh" (Psa 73:26; 84:2; Eze 44:7, 9); "body and spirit" (1Co 7:34; 2Co 7:1); "vexation from your heart … pain from your body" (Ecc 11:10); [Claude reading] Wholeness is expressed by *adding* terms, not by defining parts. observations.text: In 1Kgs.22.8, 2Chr.18.7, Deut.13.14, and Deut.17.4 the sense of darash sits squarely within its base gloss of formal/careful inquiry (of the Lord, or of an alleged matter) with no notable divergence from the general stepGloss.

In Deut.13.14 the addressed Israelite (party, second-person singular) is commanded to initiate the inquiry, directed toward establishing the truth of a reported abomination -- an operation aimed at a matter/situation rather than a person.

In Deut.13.14 M13 (true/H0571H) and M23/M65 (certain) and M58 (abomination) co-occur; the inquiry (H1875) is the procedural means by which truth (M13) and certainty (M23) about the alleged abomination (M58) are to be established -- these M-codes describe the epistemic GOAL of the inquiry rather than a co-equal characteristic modifying it.

Since this subgroup's only member is H1875, there is no other member strong to compare it against within this pass; the cross-strong comparison task instead resolves to confirming internal coherence -- the 60 occurrences covered here (across 'Seek/inquire/inquired/require/searched/seeking') all sit within the single semantic family of deliberate, purposeful resort to a source of authority, verdict, or accountability (whether God, prophet, false deity, legal matter, or social/pastoral object of care), matching the subgroup definition of formal consultation and diligent inquiry with no genuinely divergent unrelated sense found in this batch.

The mechanism of seeking differs by context: toward God it operates through prayer/worship and prophetic mediation (1Kgs.22.8, 2Kgs.3.11 -- via a prophet); toward false gods it operates through idolatrous consultation or necromancy (1Sam.28.7, 2Kgs.1.2 -- via mediums); toward legal/moral matters it operates through investigation and testimony-checking (Deut.13.14, 17.4, 19.18 -- via diligent inquiry and witnesses). The underlying mechanism shifts between mediated divine consultation, illicit occult consultation, and forensic investigation.

The mode of operation varies markedly by context: toward God it operates via prayer, worship, and prophetic mediation (1Kgs.22.8, Ps.77.2); toward idols/mediums it operates via necromancy and consultation of the dead (1Sam.28.7, Deut.18.11, Isa.8.19); in judicial contexts it operates via formal investigation and cross-examination of witnesses (Deut.13.14, 17.4, 19.18, Judg.6.29); and toward abstract objects (justice, welfare, a lost object) it operates as diligent practical pursuit (Isa.1.17, Deut.22.2). The constitutional level engaged also varies -- from whole-hearted devotion (soul/heart level) to procedural legal action (behavioral level).

(7–8). The prayer comes "after they had eaten and drunk" (9).; After: Eli takes her for drunk (14). She answers in exact inner vocabulary: "a woman troubled in spirit … pouring out my soul before the Lord" (15). Then "Go in peace", and "her face was no longer sad" (17–18).; [Claude reading] Unheard heart-speech is misread by a human hearer as drunkenness, the merry-heart state (Batch F §7), and is heard by God. It is the sad-heart counter-case to the merry heart at a feast.

What the pattern shows [Claude reading]: "let my soul die" (30); The merry-heart threshold is the penultimate step (G §3.6).; The counter-case: the sad heart at a feast.; Hannah "would not eat … why is your heart sad?" → prays "after they had eaten and drunk" → is taken for drunk → "troubled in spirit … pouring out my soul" → face no longer sad (1Sa 1:7–18).; Nehemiah: "when wine was before him … Why is your face sad? … sadness of the heart" → prayer → request granted (Neh 2:1–5).; The sad heart at the feast is also a threshold, but what enters is prayer, and the outcome is a gift (G §8.2).; Revisit (Batch H §7.6) — the threshold pattern extended again: Esther's wine-banquets (Est 5:6–14; 7:3–8): "as they were drinking wine after the feast" (5:6) → Haman goes out "joyful and glad of heart" (5:9) → sees Mordecai → wrath → "all this is worth nothing to me" (5:13) → the gallows (5:14).; At the second banquet Esther asks for her life (7:3). The king "arose in his wrath from the wine-drinking" (7:7), and Haman begs for his life (7:7–8).; One banquet is the threshold for two outcomes: Esther's petition is granted; Haman falls.; The threshold refused at the heart: "Daniel resolved [*set on his heart*] that he would not defile himself with the king's food, or with the wine that he drank" (Dan 1:8) → "fatter in flesh" than those who ate it (1:15). Compare Uriah (point 5).; The inner sentence comes first: "if that servant says to himself, 'My master is delayed,' and begins … to eat and drink and get drunk" → the master comes "on a day when he does not expect him" (Luk 12:45–46; Mat 24:48–51).; The warning: "watch yourselves lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness" (Luk 21:34).; The counter-statement: "the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit" (Rom 14:17).; Revisit (Batch G v3 §16) — the threshold and death: Nabal's sequel: the heart dies in the morning (1Sa 25:37), and "about ten days later the Lord struck Nabal, and he died" (25:38). The dead heart comes before the dead man.

verses.text: Then the king answered the woman, “ Do not hide from me anything I ask you.” And the woman said, “Let my lord the king speak.”

observations.text: *kachad* H3582, hide / cut off (25) | Psa 40:10 "I have not hidden your deliverance within my heart" | Truth withheld or spoken: Jos 7:19; 1Sa 3:17–18; 2Sa 14:18; Jer 38:14, 25; Job 15:18; 27:11; Psa 78:4. Holding back speech is an inner withholding, and the heart is where it is held | The cut off / destroy sense (Exo 9:15; 23:23; 1Ki 13:34; 2Ch 32:21; Job 4:7; 22:20; Psa 83:4): no inner being. The Zec 11 "flesh" links belong to this sense and are spurious

(b) Demanding or giving full disclosure between persons.; Samuel "was afraid to tell the vision to Eli" (1Sa 3:15). Eli binds him with an oath, "Do not hide it from me" (3:17). "Samuel told him everything and hid nothing from him. And he said, 'It is the Lord. Let him do what seems good to him'" (3:18). Fear of telling is overcome, and the disclosure is met by submission.; Jonathan: "my father does nothing either great or small without disclosing it to me. And why should my father hide this from me?" (1Sa 20:2). This is trust in a father's openness, and chapter 20 proves it misplaced.; Kings demanding it: "Do not hide from me anything I ask you" (2Sa 14:18); "I will ask you a question; hide nothing from me" (Jer 38:14).; Under threat: "hide nothing from us and we will not put you to death" (Jer 38:25).; Disclosure of utter need: "We will not hide from my lord that our money is all spent … nothing left … but our bodies and our land" (Gen 47:18).

Seat.; In the verse, the bearer's own (genuine): Psa 40:10 "I have not hidden your deliverance within my heart". Batch A v3 §6 ("The heart can conceal or not"). The heart is the place where a word could be kept back, and the verse says it was not.; In the verse, the offender's own self: Isa 3:9 "they have brought evil on themselves [*their nephesh*]". Batch D v2 §2.3 ("Evil against one's own soul"). Seat-sense: *nephesh* is here the self, reflexively, and it passes the check in that sense. New in v3: the verse holds the phenomenon and its outcome together. The face does *not* conceal ("they do not hide it"), and the evil disclosed comes back on the self that disclosed it. Shamelessness is not a safe disclosure.; In the next verse, the other party's (genuine): Num 5:13 → 5:14 "the spirit of jealousy comes over him". The deed is hidden in the wife; the seat that registers it is the husband's spirit (v2).; A seat outside M47: Job 31:33 *chob*, "bosom", where the iniquity would be hidden (v1 §3 item 6; not an M47 word).; In the passage, the bearer's own — new in v3: Job 6:10 ("This would be my comfort … for I have not denied the words of the Holy One") is flanked by two uses of *nephesh*: "My appetite refuses to touch them; they are as food that is loathsome to me" (6:7). *Nephesh* is appetite here. The sense passes the check only as bodily desire, and it has turned to loathing.; "What is my strength, that I should wait? And what is my end, that I should be patient?" (6:11). *Nephesh* is inside the English "be patient", literally "lengthen my soul". It is genuine, and the soul cannot endure.; Job's one comfort, that he has not concealed God's words, stands between an appetite that loathes and a soul that can no longer wait. Not concealing is the one thing left intact.; Spurious context link: 2Sa 14:18 → 14:19 "As surely as you live [*nephesh*]" is an oath formula. Batch G v3 §4 read the formula as "the soul as what one swears by". It says nothing of the disclosure.; Whose seat, strand (b) and (e): none. The disclosures of Samuel, the kings' demands, the treasure-finder's joy and the servant's fear are all carried by speech and act, not by a seat word.

verses.text: But he himself went a day’s journey into the wilderness and came and sat down under a broom tree. And he asked that he might die, saying, “It is enough; now, O Lord, take away my life, for I am no better than my fathers.”

observations.text: Revisit (delta) — Elijah under the broom tree (context 1Ki 19:1–8): Jezebel: "if I do not make your life as the life of one of them" (2); "he was afraid, and he arose and ran for his life" (3); "he asked that he might die [*asked his nephesh to die*] … 'It is enough; now, O Lord, take away my life, for I am no better than my fathers'" (4); "he lay down and slept … an angel touched him and said, 'Arise and eat'" (5); A cake and a jar of water; "he ate and drank and lay down again" (6); "Arise and eat, for the journey is too great for you" (7); "he went in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights to Horeb" (8); [Claude reading]; He runs to save his life, then asks for it to be taken. Fear for the life and weariness of the life follow each other within a day.; The death-wish is answered with food, not with argument. The questions come later, at Horeb ("What are you doing here?", 19:9).; This is the eating-and-drinking threshold of Batch F §7, reversed. There, the meal lowers the guard and something enters. Here, the meal answers an exhausted soul and becomes strength ("the strength of that food"). Compare "strengthen your heart with a morsel of bread" (Judg 19:5; §3.1).; Four death-wishes, four answers (see §16.2 for the full set): Elijah (food), Jonah (a question about pity), Samson (granted, with strength), Saul (granted by another's hand, who then dies for it).
Elijah | "he asked that he might die … take away my life" (1Ki 19:4) | a threat to his life; flight (19:2–3) | Food from an angel, twice → strength for forty days (19:5–8) (§6)
Batch C v3 (delta) | "Life 'better' gone" (Jon 4:3, 8; 1Ki 19:4) | The before and after of these wishes are read in G §6 and §16.2. C's desire-reading stands | No change

The soul asks to die [lexical]: "he asked that he might die [*asked his nephesh to die*] … 'take away my life'" (1Ki 19:4 — Elijah); "he asked that he might die [*asked his nephesh to die*]" (Jon 4:8 — Jonah), with "a scorching east wind" [*wind*]; [Claude reading] Two prophets, the same idiom: the self asks its own soul to die.

13. Cross-cutting observations for Batch E [Claude reading]: Relating to God engages the whole inner seat, and the texts say so by formula.; "With all your heart and with all your soul" governs: serving (Deu 10:12; Jos 22:5); keeping the law and renewing the covenant (2Ki 23:3; 2Ch 34:31; Deu 30:10); loving after circumcision of heart (Deu 30:6); praying and returning (1Ki 8:48); being tested (Deu 13:3); "With my whole heart" governs thanks, praise, crying and seeking.; The formula also appears of God (Jer 32:41).; The heart is where the relation to God is located, examined and known.; It prays without voice (1Sa 1:13) and cries (Lam 2:18).; It holds the law (Psa 37:31) and trusts (Psa 28:7).; It believes (Rom 10:10) and is circumcised (Deu 30:6).; It is the organ God tests (§8.1). Knowing hearts is the ground of God's forgiveness (1Ki 8:39) and of his giving the Spirit (Act 15:8).; Where heart and lips diverge, the lips do not count (Hos 7:14; Isa 29:13).; The soul is the self in address. It is spoken to by its owner ("Bless the Lord, O my soul"; "Why are you cast down, O my soul"), and asked to be spoken to by God ("Say to my soul, 'I am your salvation'", Psa 35:3). It is also the life that is: asked for (Est 7:3; 1Ki 17:21); asked to die (1Ki 19:4; Jon 4:8); redeemed, ransomed and atoned for (§9.1, §11.1); delivered or lost (§11.3); The human spirit is most active in this batch.; It prays and sings apart from the mind (1Co 14:14–16).; It serves (Rom 1:9) and worships in spirit (Joh 4:23–24).; It rejoices in the Savior (Luk 1:47) and is renewed (Eze 36:26; Eph 4:23).; It receives the benediction "grace be with your spirit".; At death it is the part committed to God (Psa 31:5; Luk 23:46; Act 7:59; Mat 27:50).; Its complaint voices anguish (Job 7:11), and its brokenness blocks hearing (Exo 6:9).; The divine Spirit relates to God on the person's behalf.; It cries "Abba" in the heart (Gal 4:6) and intercedes within the searched heart (Rom 8:26–27).; It bears witness (Heb 10:15) and writes on hearts (2Co 3:3).; It circumcises the heart (Rom 2:29) and renews (Tit 3:5).; It gives faith and gifts (1Co 12:9; Gal 3:2) and speaks through the prophet (2Sa 23:2).; It can itself be tested (Act 5:9), resisted (Act 7:51) and outraged (Heb 10:29).; Other spirits relate to God too, and are judged by that relation.

The human soul's revulsion at food, before death: "we loathe this worthless food" (Num 21:5); "they loathed any kind of food, and they drew near to the gates of death" (Psa 107:18); "his life loathes bread" (Job 33:20).; Revisit (Batch G v3 §16.2): each of these is followed by a turn: Num 21: serpents → "when he sees it, shall live" (21:8–9); Psa 107: "they cried to the Lord … He sent out his word and healed them" (107:19–20); Job 33: a mediator's ransom → "let his flesh become fresh" (33:24–25); Set beside them, Elijah's death-wish is answered with food (1Ki 19:4–8).

What the pattern shows [Claude reading]: The threshold entered with death in view: the Lord "called for weeping and mourning … and behold, joy and gladness … eating flesh and drinking wine. 'Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.'" → "this iniquity will not be atoned for you until you die" (Isa 22:12–14). The feast is held against a call to mourn.; The threshold reversed: Elijah asks to die (1Ki 19:4) → "Arise and eat" (19:5, 7) → "in the strength of that food" to Horeb (19:8). Here the meal does not lower the guard. It carries an exhausted soul across from wanting to die to going on.
Life "better" gone: "take my life from me, for it is better for me to die" (Jon 4:3, 8); "take away my life, for I am no better than my fathers" (1Ki 19:4).
Face: S03 The soul dies, or asks to die; Hits: 15; Example: Num 23:10; Judg 16:30; Eze 18:4, 20; 1Ki 19:4; Jon 4:3, 8

Meaning: *nephesh* ("soul, life") is used of the one who dies. It is not only something that leaves at death. Implies: Ch 2's "The soul departs" (Gen 35:18) is one face only. The same word is also the subject of dying.

verses.text: When they had crossed, Elijah said to Elisha, “ Ask what I shall do for you, before I am taken from you.” And Elisha said, “ Please let there be a double portion of your spirit on me.”

observations.text: 2Ki 2:2–6 | Elijah: "Please stay here" (three times) | Elisha: "As the Lord lives, and as you yourself live, I will not leave you" (three times) | "Let there be a double portion of your spirit on me" (2:9) → "The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha" (2:15; Batch F §9.5)

Asking for another's spirit: "'Ask what I shall do for you' … 'Please let there be a double portion of your spirit on me'" (2Ki 2:9) [H2]. A human spirit is the object of petition, and it is transferable.; Revisit 2026-09-28: the outcome in context: the request is granted on condition of *seeing* Elijah taken (2:10); Elisha's first act is a question: "Where is the Lord, the God of Elijah?" (2:14); others then recognise it: "The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha" (2:15); See Batch F §9.5.

13. Cross-cutting observations for Batch E [Claude reading]: Unclean spirits recognise the Son of God (Mar 3:11) and obey him (Mar 1:27).; Spirits either confess Jesus come in the flesh or are "the spirit of the antichrist" (1Jo 4:2–3).; They must be tested (1Jo 4:1), and the spirit of error stands against the Spirit of truth (1Jo 4:6).; The Lord can dispatch a lying spirit (1Ki 22:23). Ministering spirits serve (Heb 1:14).; Flesh in relating to God: "All flesh" is humanity as it comes to God: all flesh comes in prayer (Psa 65:2), sees salvation and glory (Luk 3:6; Isa 40:5), and blesses (Psa 145:21).; Covenant is cut in the flesh, and its inner counterpart is the circumcised heart (§7.2).; Flesh vs spirit as powers: Isa 31:3; Joh 6:63; 1Co 5:5; Jer 17:5.; The "life of the flesh is in the blood" (Lev 17:11) is the ground of atonement.; God is shown with his own heart and soul in these relations: his soul avenges (Jer 5:9) and he swears by it (Amo 6:8); he acts with all his heart and soul (Jer 32:41); he wishes for a heart in his people (Deu 5:29); his heart recoils in compassion (Hos 11:8); his soul delights in the servant (Isa 42:1); he gives up the beloved of his soul (Jer 12:7); the priest acts according to his heart and soul (1Sa 2:35); Speech and the heart. The heart speaks inwardly ("in the heart", §1.3), is spoken to ("to the heart" = comfort, §1.4), and its speech either matches the mouth or is betrayed by it. Hebrew prayer is an act of the heart that may or may not reach the lips.; Fringe worth keeping: *kāvôd* as the inner self (§3.2) — a possible inner-being term outside M47; the soul asked to die (§2); the double portion of another's spirit (2Ki 2:9); the dying soul naming a child and the returning spirit naming a spring (§1.8); Isaac's soul giving the blessing (§12); Qoheleth testing his own heart (Ecc 2:1); the Gentile's heart-and-conscience law-court (Rom 2:15); the flesh-then-breath sequence of the dry bones (Eze 37:6–8); "gain the whole world and forfeit his soul" (Mat 16:26); "transgression speaks [as an oracle] deep in his heart" (Psa 36:1); the heart with "highways to Zion" (Psa 84:5); "absent in body … present in spirit" (Col 2:5)
Revisit: Batch E §2 recorded 2Ki 2:9 only as "asking for another's spirit". Its outcome in 2:15 is part of the same relation.

3.8 The inner seat shared or joined between persons ◆ fringe cluster: *Soul to soul:*; "the soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul" (1Sa 18:1, 3; 20:17); "your friend who is as your own soul" (Deu 13:6, with "the wife you embrace"); "his life is bound up in the boy's life" (Gen 44:30); *Heart to heart:* "my heart will be joined to you" (1Ch 12:17); "Is your heart true to my heart as mine is to yours?" (2Ki 10:15); "you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together" (2Co 7:3); "I hold you in my heart" (Phili 1:7); "in person not in heart" (1Th 2:17).; *Shared across a group:* "one heart and soul" (Act 4:32); "one spirit, with one mind" (Phili 1:27); "Did we not act in the same spirit?" (2Co 12:18).; *Transferred between persons:* "a double portion of your spirit" (2Ki 2:9, 15); "take some of the Spirit that is on you and put it on them" (Num 11:17, 25); "in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children" (Luk 1:17; Mal 4:6).; *Captured or stolen by others:* "Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel" (2Sa 15:6); "his wives turned away his heart" (1Ki 11:3); "he swayed the heart of all the men of Judah as one man" (2Sa 19:14).; *Known from shared experience:* "You know the heart [nephesh] of a sojourner, for you were sojourners" (Exo 23:9).; *With a spouse:* "guard yourselves in your spirit, and let none of you be faithless to the wife of your youth" (Mal 2:15–16); "one flesh" (Gen 2:24).; [Claude reading] The inner seat is not depicted as sealed inside the individual. It can be knit to, joined with, held within, carried in, stolen by, or shared with another person. It can also be passed from one person to another (spirit).

verses.text: And he said, “You have asked a hard thing; yet, if you see me as I am being taken from you, it shall be so for you, but if you do not see me, it shall not be so.”

observations.text: 9. Cross-cutting observations for Batch B [Claude reading]: The heart is the organ of attention, knowing, understanding, storing, remembering and reasoning. Attention is literally *setting the heart*. The heart's hardness is the same thing as failing to hear and understand.; The soul relates to knowledge by *receiving* it (pleasant, sweet, life-giving) and by dwelling on memories (bowed down). The soul can be commanded to remember. Soul-desire can run ahead of knowledge.; The human spirit is the seat of self-knowledge and searching. It knows a person's thoughts, makes understanding possible as God's breath in man, searches after the heart meditates, and perceives others' inner reasoning. A cool spirit (temper) is linked with understanding and restrained speech.; God's Spirit is the true source of knowledge, wisdom, skill, teaching, remembrance and prophecy. The heart or own spirit as a source of prophecy is condemned.; Hearing is the main channel into the inner seat. The ear receives; the heart keeps, understands or refuses. News makes hearts melt, spirits revive and souls refresh. God hears the heart. The "hearing heart" of 1 Kgs 3:9 is confirmed in the tags.; Revisit 2026-09-28: the context reads add two qualifications.; Hearing sometimes needs seeing. Jacob's spirit revives only when he sees the wagons (Gen 45:27, Batch G §2). Elisha receives the spirit on condition of seeing (2Ki 2:10, Batch F §9.5).; What is heard moves between people. Esau's heart-speech is reported (Gen 27:42, Batch F §8.2). A fainthearted soldier melts others (Deu 20:8, Batch F §6).; Word and breath belong together: creative word // breath of his mouth; Spirit and words in the mouth; empty words are "wind".; Flesh appears as a *way of knowing and judging* ("according to the flesh"), set against revelation from the Father and the Spirit.; Soul-ish vs spiritual (§8) is a genuine textual contrast between the soul and spirit orders, and it touches the open question from depiction v1.

2. Revival — the spirit returns: "Alive" runs through the scene: the son is alive (26, 28), the father's spirit comes alive (27), and the father now speaks of his own death (28).; As in 2Ki 2:10–15 (Batch F §9.5), seeing is the hinge.

Asking for another's spirit: "'Ask what I shall do for you' … 'Please let there be a double portion of your spirit on me'" (2Ki 2:9) [H2]. A human spirit is the object of petition, and it is transferable.; Revisit 2026-09-28: the outcome in context: the request is granted on condition of *seeing* Elijah taken (2:10); Elisha's first act is a question: "Where is the Lord, the God of Elijah?" “And I, Artaxerxes the king, make a decree to all the treasurers in the province Beyond the River: Whatever Ezra the priest, the scribe of the Law of the God of heaven, requires of you, let it be done with all diligence,

observations.text: This occurrence matches the term's usual adverbial sense of thorough/eager diligence used in royal decrees; no divergence from its typical use.

Diligence responds to Ezra's requiring (M21), itself backed by the king's decree (M72); diligence is the compliance standard, not the source, of the chain -- same party (treasurers) enacts it in response to both.

The operation 'done' (T3) is to be carried out by the treasurers 'with all diligence' -- diligence qualifies how the treasurers (initiators of the action, though responding to Ezra's demand) direct their compliance toward fulfilling the requirement.

H0629 (Ezra.6.8, 6.12, 6.13, 7.17, 7.21) and H0149 (Ezra.7.23) both surface in the same Ezra decree-cycle, both are pure adverbs (AD) with no nominal/verbal form, and both attach to acts of provisioning or executing a royal/divine command -- confirming the two strongs occupy the same narrow administrative niche of 'thoroughness of compliance' rather than distinct semantic territories.

Morphologically, both H0149 and H0629 are invariant adverbs (AD) across every occurrence in this subgroup -- there is no stem/voice variation to check for meaning-relevance in either term; both are fixed adverbial intensifiers with no active/passive/causative distinction possible, a genuine no-distinction-found result for the morph-reading requirement.

The immediate response denoted (complete, prompt execution of a command) is consistent across every occurrence of both strongs -- payment 'in full without delay' (6.8), decree carried out 'with all diligence' (6.12, 7.21, 6.13), building progressing 'diligently' (5.8), purchase/offering 'with all diligence' (7.17), judgment executed 'strictly' (7.26), and compliance 'in full' (7.23) all show the same uniform thoroughness-response, varying only in the domain of the act, not in the quality of response.

Yes -- the characteristic consistently operates through a communicative/decree-based mode: it qualifies compliance with an explicit royal or divine decree ('I make a decree... let it be done with all diligence,' 6.12; 'I make a decree... let it be done with all diligence,' 7.21; 'whatever is decreed... let it be done in full,' 7.23) -- the diligence/fullness is always the response to a spoken/written command, never a self-originated act.

No movement across constitutional levels or from an external spirit is shown -- the characteristic moves entirely at the level of external administrative behavior, originating from a decree (spoken/written command) and terminating in an external act of compliance, with no mention of internal transmission through spirit, soul, or body. Record none for internal movement.

No prior reception or becoming is described before a person extends the characteristic -- treasurers and governors are simply commanded by decree to comply; there is no narrated transformation or endowment that precedes their giving.

The characteristic consistently co-occurs with decree/authority vocabulary (H4430 king, H5648 done/executed) and with terms for royal or divine wrath/judgment (H7109 wrath in 7.23; judicial penalty terms in 7.26) -- these adjacent characteristics of authority and consequence appear in nearly every occurrence, showing the diligence-term is never isolated but always framed by a command-and-consequence structure.

The characteristic consistently follows a decree/command in sequence -- in every occurrence a decree is issued first ('I make a decree...', 'whatever is decreed...') and the diligence/fullness term describes the response that follows; the sequence is always command-then-compliance, never the reverse.

The characteristic is produced by an issued decree/command -- it does not arise spontaneously but is generated as the required response to an authoritative order (royal decree in 6.12/6.13/7.21/7.26; divine decree in 7.17/7.23).

observations.text: Deuteronomy 12:18: "And you shall rejoice before the Lord your God in all that you undertake": The chapter opens by clearing away the places of the nations: *"You shall surely destroy all the places where the nations whom you shall dispossess served their gods"* (v2). Then: *"You shall not worship the Lord your God in that way. But you shall seek the place that the Lord your God will choose"* (v4–5). Two measures are set against each other: *"You shall not do according to all that we are doing here today, everyone doing whatever is right in his own eyes"* (v8). The place God chooses replaces the places a person sees for himself: *"Take care that you do not offer your burnt offerings at any place that you see, but at the place that the Lord will choose"* (v13–14).; Rejoicing is commanded three times in the chapter, each time at the chosen place and *"before the Lord"*: *"there you shall eat before the Lord your God, and you shall rejoice, you and your households, in all that you undertake, in which the Lord your God has blessed you"* (v7); *"you shall rejoice before the Lord your God, you and your sons and your daughters, your male servants and your female servants, and the Levite that is within your towns, since he has no portion or inheritance with you"* (v12); *"you shall eat them before the Lord your God in the place that the Lord your God will choose, you and your son and your daughter, your male servant and your female servant, and the Levite … And you shall rejoice before the Lord your God in all that you undertake"* (v18); The ground of the joy is named in v7: *"in which the Lord your God has blessed you"*. The place is where the joy is had. The blessing is what it is about.; The joy is not had alone. The household, the servants and the Levite are named in it each time. The verse after v18 turns the same thought into a warning: *"Take care that you do not neglect the Levite as long as you live in your land"* (v19).

observations.text: The data (135): 57 have no other M-code. These are the tabernacle and temple measurements, the pillars, Goliath, the gallows, high places and gates; 78 have another M-code, but the height word takes no part in it. For example, "the upper gate" stands beside a king, and "a high mountain" beside the Transfiguration; 25 are God, or Christ, "on high" with no other M-code joined. Examples are Psa 92:8, Psa 97:9, Heb 1:3 and Luk 24:49 ("power from on high"). They are noted in the CSV so that 13.1 can draw on them if wanted; Five are the tree and cedar figures of Eze 31:3, 31:5 and Dan 4:10, 11, 20. The pride in those passages is named in other verses (Eze 31:10; Dan 4:30, 37), and those verses are kept as P; Seven data verses are cited in the narrative: Eze 13:18, 1Sa 28:20, Job 25:2, Isa 24:18, Est 5:14, Psa 113:5 and Isa 7:11. Setting them aside here does not touch those citations. Each was cited for another word in the verse.

Data only: the sleep words in their ordinary sense, and other senses (15): Gen 2:21; 41:5; Judg 16:14; Psa 4:8; Pro 4:16; Isa 5:27; Eze 34:25; Luk 22:45; Act 12:6; Jer 51:57 (the same; oracle as Jer 51:39, which the narrative cites); Lev 13:11 ("chronic") and Lev 26:10 ("long kept"), where; H3462 is not *sleep*; Isa 7:11 and Job 11:8 (Sheol as a measure of depth); Isa 57:9.

Isaiah 7:15–16 — "when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good": The setting is a king’s heart in fear. Syria and Ephraim are marching on Jerusalem, and *"the heart of Ahaz and the heart of his people shook as the trees of the forest shake before the wind"* (v2). The Lord sends Isaiah with a word for that heart: *"Be careful, be quiet, do not fear, and do not let your heart be faint"* (v4); the threat *"shall not stand"* (v7); then the condition: *"If you are not firm in faith, you will not be firm at all"* (v9). Both "firm" words are the one verb (H0539), so standing firm and being kept firm are the same word.; Then the Lord makes Ahaz an offer: *"Ask a sign of the Lord your God; let it be deep as Sheol or high as heaven"* (v11). Ahaz refuses, in pious words: *"I will not ask, and I will not put the Lord to the test"* (v12). The answer shows what that refusal was: *"Is it too little for you to weary men, that you weary my God also?"* (v13). Ahaz’s refusal was a choice. He chose not to take hold of what the Lord held out.; The sign is given anyway, and at its centre is a child who has what Ahaz lacked: *"He shall eat curds and honey when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"* (v15). The act is one act with two sides: refusing the evil (H3988A); choosing the good (H0977); Refusing is not a step before the choice. It is the choice seen from the other side. Both rest on a knowing: *"when he knows how"*. The verse marks the moment a person can tell evil from good and turn from the one to the other.; The verse ties the eating to that knowing: he eats *"when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"*. The oracle itself says what curds and honey are. *"In that day … because of the abundance of milk that they give, he will eat curds, for everyone who is left in the land will eat curds and honey"* (v21–22). It is the food of those left in the land after the Lord has swept it with *"the king of Assyria"*: vineyards turned to *"briers and thorns"*, hills *"where cattle are let loose"* (v23–25). The child who refuses the evil and chooses the good eats with those who are left, and eats from abundance, in a land stripped of what it had.

observations.text: Led to: Ahaz refuses the sign the Lord offers: *"I will not ask, and I will not put the Lord to the test"* (v12). So *"the Lord himself will give you a sign … Immanuel"* (v14).

Isaiah 43:10: "my servant whom I have chosen, that you may know and believe me and understand": The setting is a court. The nations are summoned: *"All the nations gather together … Let them bring their witnesses to prove them right"* (v9). Israel is brought out as the Lord's witness, and described as unfit for it: *"Bring out the people who are blind, yet have eyes, who are deaf, yet have ears!"* (v8).; Then: *"You are my witnesses," declares the Lord, "and my servant whom I have chosen, that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he"* (v10). The knowing, believing and understanding are the purpose of the choosing. They are not its ground. The chosen were blind and deaf when chosen. They were chosen in order to come to know.; This is the reverse of the order in §2a, where the child chooses *"when he knows how"* (Isa 7:15). There the knowing comes before the person's own choosing. Here, the knowing follows God's choosing of the person. Each verse states its own order.; What the chosen are to know is one thing: *"that I am he. Before me no god was formed"* (v10). The Lord's own witness follows: *"I declared and saved and proclaimed, when there was no strange god among you"* (v12).; The oracles that follow set the chosen beside those who make idols: The chosen people do not perceive what God is doing: *"Behold, I am doing a new thing; now it springs forth, do you not perceive it?"* (43:19). "Perceive" is the same word as "know" in v10 (H3045).; The idol-makers' witnesses *"neither see nor know"* (44:9).; Of the idol-maker himself: *"They know not, nor do they discern, for he has shut their eyes, so that they cannot see, and their hearts, so that they cannot understand"* (44:18). "Know" and "discern" are the same words as "know" and "understand" in 43:10 (H3045, H0995).; The chosen people are also accused: *"Yet you did not call upon me, O Jacob; but you have been weary of me, O Israel!"* (43:22); *"you have burdened me with your sins; you have wearied me with your iniquities"* (43:24). Then comes the answer: *"I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins"* (43:25).

Ahaz refuses, in pious words: *"I will not ask, and I will not put the Lord to the test"* (v12). The answer shows what that refusal was: *"Is it too little for you to weary men, that you weary my God also?"* (v13). Ahaz’s refusal was a choice. He chose not to take hold of what the Lord held out.; The sign is given anyway, and at its centre is a child who has what Ahaz lacked: *"He shall eat curds and honey when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"* (v15). The act is one act with two sides: refusing the evil (H3988A); choosing the good (H0977); Refusing is not a step before the choice. It is the choice seen from the other side. Both rest on a knowing: *"when he knows how"*. The verse marks the moment a person can tell evil from good and turn from the one to the other.; The verse ties the eating to that knowing: he eats *"when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"*. The oracle itself says what curds and honey are. *"In that day … because of the abundance of milk that they give, he will eat curds, for everyone who is left in the land will eat curds and honey"* (v21–22). It is the food of those left in the land after the Lord has swept it with *"the king of Assyria"*: vineyards turned to *"briers and thorns"*, hills *"where cattle are let loose"* (v23–25). The child who refuses the evil and chooses the good eats with those who are left, and eats from abundance, in a land stripped of what it had.

Choosing has two sides: Refusing is itself choosing. The child *"knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"* (Isa 7:15). The oracle around that verse shows refusing going both ways. Ahaz refuses the Lord's offer of a sign with pious words: *"I will not ask, and I will not put the Lord to the test"* (Isa 7:12). The people *"refused the waters of Shiloah that flow gently"* (8:6). The right refusing and the wrong refusing are set in one oracle, each with its own consequence.; Not answering is already choosing. *"when I called, you did not answer; when I spoke, you did not listen, but you did what was evil in my eyes and chose what I did not delight in"* (Isa 65:12; repeated in 66:4). The choosing of what the Lord does not delight in is where the not-listening ends up.; The choice is laid out with both its sides and both its ends: *"cease to do evil, learn to do good"*; *"If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land"*; *"but if you refuse and rebel, you shall be eaten by the sword"* (Isa 1:16–20).

file_lines.section: An inner act weighed by what God chooses
file_lines.text: In one passage the inner act of the others is itself set against God's choosing. The people fast and ask, *"Why have we humbled ourselves, and you take no knowledge of it?"* (Isa 58:3). They *"delight to know my ways"* and *"delight to draw near to God"* (58:2). Yet *"in the day of your fast you seek your own pleasure, and oppress all your workers"* (58:3). Then: *"Is such the fast that I choose, a day for a person to humble himself?"* (58:5). "Humble himself" is the humbling of the soul, the same words as their own complaint. What God does choose is turned outward: *"to let the oppressed go free"*, *"to share your bread with the hungry"*, *"not to hide yourself from your own flesh"* (58:6–7).

verses.text: I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me; I was ready to be found by those who did not seek me. I said, “ Here I am, here I am,” to a nation that was not called by my name.

observations.text: No other M-code characteristic co-occurs in this verse alongside the seeking of the priesthood.

God is the initiator here ('by those who did not seek me' being sought BY God), an inversion where God is subject seeking out a nation that itself did not seek him -- the direction is God toward the unresponsive nation.

M42 (called, H7121H) co-occurs describing the nation not being 'called by God's name'; it characterizes the unresponsive nation's identity, distinct from the inquiring/seeking dynamic itself which here is enacted by God, not the nation.

In Isa.65.1 God's readiness to be sought by those who did not ask reveals his own disposition/perception that he is available and near even to those not yet oriented toward him -- a divine self-disclosure of gracious accessibility rather than a human perception.

God's extension of the characteristic (his willingness to be sought/found) is shown as both conditional and responsive: conditional on genuine seeking ('If you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever', 1Chr.28.9), yet also shown as gracious and unconditioned in Isa.65.1 ('I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me') -- God's self-disclosure as available to be inquired of exceeds strict conditionality, showing both a covenantal-conditional pattern and a gracious-responsive pattern.

God's extension of the characteristic -- his readiness to be sought even by those who did not ask (Isa.65.1) and his invitation 'Seek me and live' (Amos.5.4) -- shows a disposition of gracious accessibility and desire for relationship with humanity, contrasted with his refusal to be inquired of by the unrepentant and idolatrous (Ezek.20.3, 20.31), revealing a disposition that is both inviting and holy/discerning.

Isaiah 65:12 — "chose what I did not delight in": This is an oracle. It opens with God, not with the people: *"I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me … I said, “Here I am, here I am,”"* (v1); *"I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people, who walk in a way that is not good, following their own devices"* (v2); The wrong choosing in v12 is made in front of a God who is calling and holding out his hands.; The oracle shows what they turned to instead: sacrifices *"in gardens"*, sitting *"in tombs"*, eating *"pig’s flesh"* (v3–4); a pride that says *"do not come near me, for I am too holy for you"* (v5); they *"forget my holy mountain"* and *"set a table for Fortune and fill cups of mixed wine for Destiny"* (v11); They put their trust in luck and fate.; The answer turns on their own word: *"I will destine you to the sword"* (v12). In Hebrew, "Destiny" (Meni, H4507) and "destine" (manah, H4487) come from the same root. They poured cups for Destiny, and the Lord destines them. What they chose to trust becomes the form their judgement takes.; The verse then gives the reason, and the reason is in the inner being: *"because, when I called, you did not answer; when I spoke, you did not listen, but you did what was evil in my eyes and chose what I did not delight in."* The choosing does not stand alone. It is the far end of not answering and not listening. When they turned away from the voice calling them, that was already a choice, and choosing what God does not delight in is where it ends.; There is a phrase to set beside Joshua 24. There, the choice turned on what was *"evil in your eyes"*. Here they *"did what was evil in my eyes"*. The measure has moved from their eyes to God's, and his delight is the standard their choice is judged by.; In the same oracle the word "chosen" is used of the others: *"my chosen shall possess it"* (v9); *"You shall leave your name to my chosen for a curse"* (v15); So in one passage there are those who chose what God did not delight in, and those God calls *"my chosen"*. The outcome sets the two side by side and reaches the inner being on both sides: *"my servants shall sing for gladness of heart, but you shall cry out for pain of heart and shall wail for breaking of spirit"* (v14). The choice ends in the heart and spirit of the one who made it.

Choosing before a God who has already acted: In these verses the human choice is never the first move.; At Shechem it comes after eleven verses of what the Lord did, beginning with *"I took your father Abraham from beyond the River"* (Jos 24:3).; In Isaiah 65 the wrong choice is made in front of a God who says *"Here I am, here I am"* and *"I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people"* (65:1–2).; At the Jerusalem council the church's choosing follows Peter's word that *"God made a choice among you"* (Act 15:7), in the same verb.

observations.text: Part 2 verses: what they add. The four strands hold, and each gains an instance: Strand (a), a demand no one can meet, with the angry one now the demander. "There is not a man on earth who can meet the king's demand … no one can show it to the king except the gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh" (Dan 2:10–11). Then "Because of this the king was angry and very furious, and commanded that all the wise men of Babylon be destroyed" (2:12). This is the mirror of Gen 30:2. Jacob, faced with an impossible demand, named God as the only one who could meet it. Nebuchadnezzar hears the same answer ("except the gods") and orders a massacre; The anger is answered by "prudence and discretion" (Dan 2:14): Daniel's; Strand (b), thwarted and made a fool of. "Herod, when he saw that he had been tricked by the wise men, became furious, and he sent and killed all the male children" (Mat 2:16). "Tricked" is Balaam's "you have made a fool of me" (Num 22:29). This time the killing is carried out, and it ends in "Rachel weeping for her children; she refused to be comforted" (Mat 2:18); Strand (d), refused by subordinates; Nebuchadnezzar "in furious rage" at the three who "do not serve your gods" (Dan 3:12–13); After their answer, "But if not … we will not serve your gods" (3:18), "Nebuchadnezzar was filled with fury, and the expression of his face was changed against Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. He ordered the furnace heated seven times more" (3:19); The face changes outward, against them. This is the reverse of §1's fallen face, which turns inward; The outcome reverses the anger: "Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego … who trusted in him, and set aside the king's command" (3:28). The king blesses the very refusal that enraged him; A new instance, thwarted from outside and turned against the weaker: "ships of Kittim shall come against him, and he shall be afraid and withdraw, and shall turn back and be enraged and take action against the holy covenant" (Dan 11:30). "News from the east and the north shall alarm him, and he shall go out with great fury to destroy" (11:44). Fear comes first, then anger. The anger is turned on a weaker target than the one that thwarted him.

file_lines.section: 4. Anger when one's will is blocked, exposed or refused (TH) — 17 verses
file_lines.text: - **Strand (a), a demand no one can meet, with the angry one now the demander.** "There is not a man on earth who can meet the king's demand … no one can show it to the king except the gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh" (Dan 2:10–11). Then "Because of this the king was angry and very furious, and commanded that all the wise men of Babylon be destroyed" (2:12). **This is the mirror of Gen 30:2.** Jacob, faced with an impossible demand, named God as the only one who could meet it. Nebuchadnezzar hears the same answer ("except the gods") and orders a massacre.

verses.text: The thing that the king asks is difficult, and no one can show it to the king except the gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh.”

observations.text: Part 2 verses: what they add. The four strands hold, and each gains an instance: Strand (a), a demand no one can meet, with the angry one now the demander. "There is not a man on earth who can meet the king's demand … no one can show it to the king except the gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh" (Dan 2:10–11). Then "Because of this the king was angry and very furious, and commanded that all the wise men of Babylon be destroyed" (2:12). This is the mirror of Gen 30:2. Jacob, faced with an impossible demand, named God as the only one who could meet it. Nebuchadnezzar hears the same answer ("except the gods") and orders a massacre; The anger is answered by "prudence and discretion" (Dan 2:14): Daniel's; Strand (b), thwarted and made a fool of. "Herod, when he saw that he had been tricked by the wise men, became furious, and he sent and killed all the male children" (Mat 2:16). "Tricked" is Balaam's "you have made a fool of me" (Num 22:29). This time the killing is carried out, and it ends in "Rachel weeping for her children; she refused to be comforted" (Mat 2:18); Strand (d), refused by subordinates; Nebuchadnezzar "in furious rage" at the three who "do not serve your gods" (Dan 3:12–13); After their answer, "But if not … we will not serve your gods" (3:18), "Nebuchadnezzar was filled with fury, and the expression of his face was changed against Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. He ordered the furnace heated seven times more" (3:19); The face changes outward, against them. This is the reverse of §1's fallen face, which turns inward; The outcome reverses the anger: "Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego … who trusted in him, and set aside the king's command" (3:28). The king blesses the very refusal that enraged him; A new instance, thwarted from outside and turned against the weaker: "ships of Kittim shall come against him, and he shall be afraid and withdraw, and shall turn back and be enraged and take action against the holy covenant" (Dan 11:30). "News from the east and the north shall alarm him, and he shall go out with great fury to destroy" (11:44). Fear comes first, then anger. The anger is turned on a weaker target than the one that thwarted him.

Seat . No in-verse seat in the six: Outside the verse: Dan 11:28 "his heart shall be set against the holy covenant". Genuine. The bearer's own, two verses before the rage. The heart was set before the thwarting. The anger only releases it; Dan 2:11 "not with flesh". Spurious as a seat: flesh as the human realm.

verses.text: And Daniel went in and requested the king to appoint him a time, that he might show the interpretation to the king.
To you, O God of my fathers, I give thanks and praise, for you have given me wisdom and might, and have now made known to me what we asked of you, for you have made known to us the king’s matter.”
Daniel answered the king and said, “ No wise men, enchanters, magicians, or astrologers can show to the king the mystery that the king has asked,
Daniel made a request of the king, and he appointed Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego over the affairs of the province of Babylon. But Daniel remained at the king’s court.

At the same time my reason returned to me, and for the glory of my kingdom, my majesty and splendor returned to me. My counselors and my lords sought me, and I was established in my kingdom, and still more greatness was added to me.

Then the high officials and the satraps sought to find a ground for complaint against Daniel with regard to the kingdom, but they could find no ground for complaint or any fault, because he was faithful, and no error or fault was found in him.

observations.text: 10.7 Choosing and setting direction, new section *Planning* | The account of looking ahead. Planning carries a choice ahead (Gen 11:6; Pro 16:9). It covers: weighing first (Luk 14:28–33; Pro 31:15–16; Judg 19:30); planning without knowing (Act 27:10–14, 39–41; Rom 1:13; Jam 4:15); a plan carrying a person's word (2Co 1:17–18); planning together and parting (Act 15:37–39; Luk 23:51–52); planning for another's good (Dan 6:3–4), with the king's planning measured against God's (2Sa 14:13–14); a purpose held (Psa 17:3, 5; Act 11:23; 2Ti 3:10; 1Ch 29:18; Rom 8:6–7; Isa 26:3); devised from one's own heart (1Ki 12:32–33; Neh 6:8); the plan and its outcome (Pro 16:9; Isa 8:10; Act 5:38–39; Psa 21:11; Dan 11:24; Gen 50:20); seen and disclosed (1Ch 28:9; 1Co 4:3–5) | New section

verses.text: All the high officials of the kingdom, the prefects and the satraps, the counselors and the governors are agreed that the king should establish an ordinance and enforce an injunction, that whoever makes petition to any god or man for thirty days, except to you, O king, shall be cast into the den of lions.
Then these men came by agreement and found Daniel making petition and plea before his God.

Then they came near and said before the king, concerning the injunction, “O king! Did you not sign an injunction, that anyone who makes petition to any god or man within thirty days except to you, O king, shall be cast into the den of lions?” The king answered and said, “The thing stands fast, according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which cannot be revoked.”

Then they answered and said before the king, “ Daniel, who is one of the exiles from Judah, pays no attention to you, O king, or the injunction you have signed, but makes his petition three times a day.”
I approached one of those who stood there and asked him the truth concerning all this. So he told me and made known to me the interpretation of the things.
My people inquire of a piece of wood, and their walking staff gives them oracles. For a spirit of whoredom has led them astray, and they have left their God to play the whore.

observations.text: Inquiry misdirected: "My people inquire of a piece of wood … For a spirit of whoredom has led them astray" (Hos 4:12) [X].

4.2 Going astray — five agents: The heart itself: "a people who go astray in their heart" (Psa 95:10); The spirit, with a way back: "those who go astray in spirit will come to understanding" (Isa 29:24) [H1]; A foreign spirit: "a spirit of whoredom has led them astray" (Hos 4:12) [X]; "The Lord has mingled within her a spirit of confusion … as a drunken man staggers" (Isa 19:14) [X]; God: "O Lord, why do you make us wander from your ways and harden our heart?" (Isa 63:17). Context 63:1–6, 15–17: this complaint follows the divine warrior's "day of vengeance was in my heart" (63:4) and a plea that "the stirring of your inner parts and your compassion are held back" (63:15). → §6.1; The loss of understanding: "He takes away understanding [*heart*] from the chiefs … and makes them wander in a trackless waste" (Job 12:24)
Spirit of whoredom [X]: "a spirit of whoredom has led them astray" (Hos 4:12); "the spirit of whoredom is within them, and they know not the Lord" (Hos 5:4)

11. Cross-cutting observations for Batch C [Claude reading]: God is shown with his own soul and heart of desire and choice: his soul delights in the chosen servant (Isa 42:1), his heart is set on the chosen house (2Ch 7:16), he seeks a man after his heart (1Sa 13:14), his heart is grieved (Gen 6:6).; Other spirits in this batch act on orientation from outside: spirit of jealousy (Num 5), spirit of whoredom (Hos 4:12; 5:4) [X]; harmful spirit from God (1Sa 16) and the spirit at work in the disobedient (Eph 2:2) [O]; the unclean spirit seeking a dwelling (Mat 12:43) [O].; Fringe worth keeping: desire as breath-hunger — "striving after wind" (§1.9); the wine-merry heart as the point of exposure (§1.6); the heart that forsakes its owner (§9.6); the spirit that cannot be retained (Ecc 8:8); fleshly vs spiritual, with its moral / neutral / positive senses (§3.3); the heart awake while the body sleeps (Song 5:2)

c. Dispositions spoken of as "spirits" that come upon or enter a person — fringe, important [Claude reading]: "the spirit of jealousy comes over him" (Num 5:14, 30); "a spirit of whoredom has led them astray … the spirit of whoredom is within them" (Hos 4:12; 5:4); "a spirit of confusion" mingled within (Isa 19:14); "a spirit of deep sleep" poured out (Isa 29:10); "a spirit of stupor" (Rom 11:8); "a spirit of justice" (Isa 28:6); "a spirit of grace and pleas for mercy" poured out (Zec 12:10); "filled with a spirit of skill" (Exo 28:3); "the spirit of wisdom" (Deu 34:9); "a spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-control" (2Ti 1:7); "the spirit of slavery … the Spirit of adoption" (Rom 8:15); "not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God" (1Co 2:12); "the spirit of uncleanness" (Zec 13:2); "a disabling spirit" that kept a woman bent over (Luk 13:11); "a spirit that makes him mute" (Mar 9:17); spirits that convulse (Mar 1:26; 9:20; Luk 9:39); [Claude reading] In these verses, "spirit" is the name for an inner disposition or condition *that arrives*. It is given, poured out, sent, mingled, or comes upon. The line between "my spirit", "a spirit" and "God's Spirit" is not always drawn by the text. Some spirits also produce bodily effects (muteness, convulsion, a bent posture).

claims.text: Idols are taken "into their hearts" (Eze 14:3–7); the heart "goes after" idols (Eze 20:16); a "spirit of whoredom" leads astray (Hos 4:12) (dep §2.1i, §2.3c)

Most "spirit of …" phrases name a disposition that comes upon a person; the verse does not name a being. The same phrasing is used for good gifts: a spirit of wisdom, skill, grace, justice. Some are given by God: "the Lord has poured out upon you a spirit of deep sleep" (Isa 29:10); the harmful spirit "from the Lord" (1Sa 16:14); God "sent an evil spirit" (Judg 9:23); the Lord "put a lying spirit" in the prophets' mouths (1Ki 22:23). 2Ti 1:7 says "God gave us a spirit not of fear". Spirit-beings are real (unclean spirits cast out; the spirit of divination, Act 16:16), but the one-to-one mapping to vice families is not in the text (SC; dep §2.3c; D §11.4)

verses.text: When the sun rose, God appointed a scorching east wind, and the sun beat down on the head of Jonah so that he was faint. And he asked that he might die and said, “It is better for me to die than to live.”

observations.text: Sequence in Jon 3:10–4:11: God relents → Jonah angry → prayer quoting "slow to anger" → asks to die → "Do you do well to be angry?" → shade, plant, worm, wind → asks to die again → "angry enough to die" → God's comparison: pity for a plant, pity for Nineveh → (no answer).

Outside the verse: Jon 4:3 "my life" and Jon 4:8 "that he might die" (nephesh). The bearer's own. Life-sense, as the thing asked to be ended. Jonah's anger takes his own nephesh as its object. This links to §9: anger turned on oneself.

Part 2 verses: what they add. The occasion widens from God striking to God's mercy, and to the consequences of one's own folly: Jonah: anger at God's mercy; The occasion: "When God saw what they did, how they turned from their evil way, God relented of the disaster" (Jon 3:10). "But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was angry" (4:1); He quotes God's own character against him: "I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, and relenting from disaster" (4:2). Pilot §2.1 read this. The anger is at the very attribute that is the opposite of anger; It asks to die: "please take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live" (4:3). After the plant withers, "It is better for me to die than to live" (4:8), and "Yes, I do well to be angry, angry enough to die" (4:9); God asks a question, as he did with Cain: "Do you do well to be angry?" (4:4, 9). Compare "Why are you angry?" (Gen 4:6). Twice in Scripture God meets a man's anger by asking about it. Both times, the question comes before a decisive act or teaching, and both times the answer is left open; God reframes by comparison: "You pity the plant … And should not I pity Nineveh …?" (4:10–11). The anger is set beside the pity the angry man feels for a plant. The book ends on God's question. Jonah's answer is not given; The heart rages at God for one's own ruin: "When a man's folly brings his way to ruin, his heart rages against the Lord" (Pro 19:3). The anger is misdirected: the cause is his own folly, and the target is God; Deprivation turns to cursing God, then darkness: "when they are hungry, they will be enraged and will speak contemptuously against their king and their God, and turn their faces upward. And they will look to the earth, but behold, distress and darkness" (Isa 8:21–22). The face turns up in anger and finds nothing, then down and finds darkness. It is set after "should not a people inquire of their God?" (8:19).

Seat : In the verse: Pro 19:3 "heart" (lev). The bearer's own. Genuine. New here: the only in-verse seat in §13 locates anger at God in the heart, and the verse says it is misdirected; Outside the verse: Jon 4:3 "my life" and Jon 4:8 "that he might die" (nephesh). The bearer's own. Life-sense, as the thing asked to be ended. Jonah's anger takes his own nephesh as its object. This links to §9: anger turned on oneself.

(v2) Jon 3:10–4:11: Sequence the text gives: God relents → Jonah angry → prayer quoting "slow to anger" → asks to die → "Do you do well to be angry?" → shade, plant, worm, wind → asks to die again → "angry enough to die" → God's comparison: pity for a plant, pity for Nineveh → (no answer).
AG §13 (Pro 19:3; Jon 4): Context seats: sense · batch · use: Pro 19:2 "desire" [nephesh] · B v3 §1.5, C v3 §1.10 · not used. Jon 4:3, 4:8 "life … that he might die" · G v3 §16.2 et al. · used.

Fainting across every component: heart: "the whole heart faint" // "the whole head is sick" (Isa 1:5); Lam 1:22; Psa 61:2; spirit [H]: Psa 142:3; 143:4; "When I remember God, I moan; when I meditate, my spirit faints" (Psa 77:3); soul: "hungry and thirsty, their soul fainted within them" (Psa 107:5); flesh: "my flesh faints for you" (Psa 63:1); life: "When my life was fainting away, I remembered the Lord, and my prayer came to you" (Jon 2:7) — fainting turns into remembering and prayer; Revisit 2026-09-28: In the same book, Jonah "was faint" under the east wind and asked to die (Jon 4:8). Fainting in ch. 2 turns to prayer; fainting in ch. 4 turns to a death-wish (Batch G §6).; For spirit-fainting in meditation (Psa 77:3), memory works either way: it deepens the fainting (Psa 77) or turns it (Psa 42:6). See Batch F §9.4.; bosom: "their life is poured out on their mothers' bosom" (Lam 2:12)
Jonah | "take my life … better for me to die than to live" (Jon 4:3, 8) | mercy to Nineveh; the loss of the plant; a scorching wind (*rûaḥ*) | A question about pity (4:10–11) (§6)
Batch C v3 (delta) | "Life 'better' gone" (Jon 4:3, 8; 1Ki 19:4) | The before and after of these wishes are read in G §6 and §16.2. C's desire-reading stands | No change

The soul asks to die [lexical]: "he asked that he might die [*asked his nephesh to die*] … 'take away my life'" (1Ki 19:4 — Elijah); "he asked that he might die [*asked his nephesh to die*]" (Jon 4:8 — Jonah), with "a scorching east wind" [*wind*]; [Claude reading] Two prophets, the same idiom: the self asks its own soul to die.

13. Cross-cutting observations for Batch E [Claude reading]: Relating to God engages the whole inner seat, and the texts say so by formula.; "With all your heart and with all your soul" governs: serving (Deu 10:12; Jos 22:5); keeping the law and renewing the covenant (2Ki 23:3; 2Ch 34:31; Deu 30:10); loving after circumcision of heart (Deu 30:6); praying and returning (1Ki 8:48); being tested (Deu 13:3); "With my whole heart" governs thanks, praise, crying and seeking.; The formula also appears of God (Jer 32:41).; The heart is where the relation to God is located, examined and known.; It prays without voice (1Sa 1:13) and cries (Lam 2:18).; It holds the law (Psa 37:31) and trusts (Psa 28:7).; It believes (Rom 10:10) and is circumcised (Deu 30:6).; It is the organ God tests (§8.1). Knowing hearts is the ground of God's forgiveness (1Ki 8:39) and of his giving the Spirit (Act 15:8).; Where heart and lips diverge, the lips do not count (Hos 7:14; Isa 29:13).; The soul is the self in address. It is spoken to by its owner ("Bless the Lord, O my soul"; "Why are you cast down, O my soul"), and asked to be spoken to by God ("Say to my soul, 'I am your salvation'", Psa 35:3). It is also the life that is: asked for (Est 7:3; 1Ki 17:21); asked to die (1Ki 19:4; Jon 4:8); redeemed, ransomed and atoned for (§9.1, §11.1); delivered or lost (§11.3); The human spirit is most active in this batch.; It prays and sings apart from the mind (1Co 14:14–16).; It serves (Rom 1:9) and worships in spirit (Joh 4:23–24).; It rejoices in the Savior (Luk 1:47) and is renewed (Eze 36:26; Eph 4:23).; It receives the benediction "grace be with your spirit".; At death it is the part committed to God (Psa 31:5; Luk 23:46; Act 7:59; Mat 27:50).; Its complaint voices anguish (Job 7:11), and its brokenness blocks hearing (Exo 6:9).; The divine Spirit relates to God on the person's behalf.; It cries "Abba" in the heart (Gal 4:6) and intercedes within the searched heart (Rom 8:26–27).; It bears witness (Heb 10:15) and writes on hearts (2Co 3:3).; It circumcises the heart (Rom 2:29) and renews (Tit 3:5).; It gives faith and gifts (1Co 12:9; Gal 3:2) and speaks through the prophet (2Sa 23:2).; It can itself be tested (Act 5:9), resisted (Act 7:51) and outraged (Heb 10:29).; Other spirits relate to God too, and are judged by that relation.

0. Data notes (short): Pre-filter — "Lord of hosts" (H6635B, M72): 28 pairs in 22 verses. This is a divine title, not dominion as a relation. The group is reported in §1.9, not dropped.; Misleading tags (noted, and not read as the cluster's sense): "choirmaster" (H5329 "to conduct", M76): 10 psalm superscriptions (Psa 9:1, 11:1, 14:1, 36:1, 42:1, 45:1, 53:1, 57:1, 62:1, 69:1). The M47 word belongs to the psalm body. The heading has no bearing on it.; "hand: power" (H3027H, M72): 49 verses. Mostly the idiom "into the hand of" (Jeremiah's "into the hand of those who seek their life"; Joshua's conquest lists). It is read as agency, and only where the hand acts on an inner component (§1.1, §1.4).; Quantity words in M46: "abundance / greatness / multitude" of iniquity or idols (Jer 13:22; Hos 9:7; Eze 14:4), "numerous" (Deu 10:22), "to no avail" (Dan 11:27), "good for nothing" (Jer 13:10), "retinue" (1Ki 10:2). None of these is about wealth.; Words in M76 and M26 used in other senses: "pity" (Psa 69:20) — *nûd*, a sympathetic shaking of the head; "intoxicated" (Pro 5:20) — *šāgâ*, see §4.2; "appointed" (Jon 4:8) and "count on" (2Co 10:2); "heart" = "midst": "the heart of the seas" (Eze 27:27).; "spokes" (Eze 10:12) is tagged hand.; The death words are outside the M-codes (see the handoff §3), as in Batch G.

6.5 ◆ Fringe (M26): "my beloved with whom my soul is well pleased. I will put my Spirit upon him, and he will proclaim justice" (Mat 12:18) [D1] — God's soul, God's Spirit and justice in one sentence; "the souls of those who had been beheaded … authority to judge was committed" (Rev 20:4); "God appointed a scorching east wind … he asked that he might die" (Jon 4:8) → Batch G §6
Life "better" gone: "take my life from me, for it is better for me to die" (Jon 4:3, 8); "take away my life, for I am no better than my fathers" (1Ki 19:4).

5. (c) Errors realigned: Ch 5, "exhaustion". Ch 5 v3 called Job 10:1, Ecc 2:17 and Jon 4:3 "a third kind of hating one's life, which is exhaustion rather than discipleship". The verses give their own ground: Job: bitterness of soul; the Preacher: "what is done under the sun was grievous to me"; Jonah: anger that God spared Nineveh (4:1–4); faintness comes only with the second wish (4:8); The frame came from M47 batch G §6. Ch 5 now gives each ground. Ch 2 already read Jonah correctly.; Ch 4, Pro 21:1. It was listed among the "materials" for the state a heart is in. It is a heart being directed, "wherever he will", and "will" is the delight word. It is now set apart in Ch 4 and placed in 13.1 *Delight*.
Placement: confirmed in Ch 2. Ch 5: to correct. Either take Jon 4:3 out of the "exhaustion" sentence or say what its ground is. Jon 4:8 fits "faint" better.

observations.text: Life by doing, and the counter-statements. "walks in the statutes of life, not doing injustice, he shall surely live"; "My covenant with him was one of life and peace … It was a covenant of fear, and he feared me"; "For it is no empty word for you, but your very life". The lawyer: "Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?" Jesus: "You have answered correctly; do this, and you will live". "If you would enter life, keep the commandments". Against these: "Now it is evident that no one is justified before God by the law, for 'The righteous shall live by faith.' But the law is not of faith, rather 'The one who does them shall live by them'"; "Moses writes about the righteousness that is based on the law, that the person who does the commandments shall live by them"; "The very commandment that promised life proved to be death to me"
Verses: Mat 19:17–22; Joh 5:40 (with 5:42–44); Rut 3:13 (with 4:4–6); 2Ti 3:12. Compared with Isa 1:19 and 1Ti 6:9 (in 10.7).

The will invited with an "if". The man asks about doing: *"what good deed must I do?"* (Mat 19:16). Jesus answers twice with the will: *"If you would enter life, keep the commandments"* (19:17); *"If you would be perfect, go, sell … and come, follow me"* (19:21); He has kept the commandments and still asks, *"What do I still lack?"* (19:20). He senses a lack. When the will is asked for the thing he holds, he *"went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions"* (19:22).; Probes: The will, the possessions and the feeling are named in one verse. The sorrow is a will that would not, while knowing what it lacked.; The disciples ask *"Who then can be saved?"* and are told, *"With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible"* (19:25–26). That fits Rom 9:16, already in 10.7: "not on human will".
