verses.text: And he vowed to her, “ Whatever you ask me, I will give you, up to half of my kingdom.”
And she went out and said to her mother, “For what should I ask?” And she said, “The head of John the Baptist.”
And she came in immediately with haste to the king and asked, saying, “I want you to give me at once the head of John the Baptist on a platter.”

observations.text: Want (M18) is the root motivating content behind the asking (M21) which is executed in haste (M67) -- want causes/drives the whole sequence, same party (the girl), same target (the king).

G4710 is exclusively nominal across all twelve of its occurrences (N-ASF, N-GSF, N-DSF forms), meaning the subgroup's noun-member consistently names diligence/zeal/haste as a possessable, giveable, or measurable quality (something one 'shows', 'has produced in you', 'puts into a heart', or is measured 'by') -- structurally opposite to G4709's pure manner-of-action adverbial function. This is the clearest grammatical-role divergence between the two subgroup members: G4710 names the THING, G4709 describes the HOW.

G4710's occurrence list shows a wider register-range than G4709's: it covers pure physical haste with no moral overtone (Mark 6:25, Herodias's daughter rushing to the king with a grim request; Luke 1:39, Mary's journey), alongside heavily moralized/evidentiary senses in the Pauline corpus (2Cor 7:11-12, 8:7-8; used as proof of sincerity of repentance or love) and paired-virtue senses (Rom 12:8, 12:11; Heb 6:11; 2Pet 1:5, chained with faith/virtue/knowledge). G4709's three occurrences, by contrast, are uniformly positive/earnest in register (pleading, searching, doing one's best) with no neutral-or-negative-context instance comparable to Mark 6:25's use for a request tied to John the Baptist's beheading -- showing G4710 tolerates a broader range of surrounding moral valence than G4709 does within this subgroup.

Varied. The immediate response ranges from urgent physical motion (Mark 6:25's rush to the king; Luke 1:39's haste to the hill country) to an urgent verbal appeal (Luke 7:4's earnest pleading) to an inward resolve to write (Jude 1:3) -- the register of the immediate response shifts by context though the urgency itself is constant.

Varies by context. In narrative contexts (Mark 6:25, Luke 1:39, Luke 7:4) the felt quality is transient urgency tied to a specific occasion. In hortatory/epistolary contexts (Rom 12:11, Heb 6:11, 2Pet 1:5) it is framed as a settled disposition to be maintained or grown into over time.

In Mark 6:25 the haste accompanies a speech-act (the daughter's request, 'saying, I want you to give me...') and in Jude 1:3 the eagerness modifies the intent to write -- both show the characteristic bound up with a communicative act, though the characteristic itself is the manner of approach/desire to speak rather than the speech content.

The pattern of occurrence shows the characteristic seated primarily at the level of will/spirit engaged in directed action, paired explicitly with 'spirit' in Rom 12:11 ('fervent in spirit') and with 'heart' in 2Cor 8:16 (placed 'into the heart of Titus'). It never engages purely bodily/sensory levels in isolation, though physical motion (haste, Mark 6:25; Luke 1:39) is its outward expression. The heart/spirit link here is expressive -- the inner earnestness expresses itself outwardly through bodily action (hurrying) or verbal/practical deeds (pleading, providing), rather than the body generating the earnestness itself.

The characteristic ends where mere physical speed without moral/relational engagement occurs (Mark 6:25's haste tied to a grim, morally neutral-to-negative request shows the term can denote sheer speed without ethical earnestness) -- it is not synonymous with recklessness or hurried carelessness, nor with love or faith themselves, which it accompanies as evidence (2Cor 8:7-8) but does not constitute.
Whole network: want (M18) is the originating volitional core, expressed through asking (M21) and carried with haste (M67) -- want's role is the root cause driving the whole chain.
The operation 'give' (role-T3, which want governs as content) is initiated by the girl's demand and directed toward the king, who is asked to give the head at once.

Haste names the manner of the girl's entrance to the king; its role is to intensify urgency in delivering her mother's demand, marking her as fully compliant and eager to press it through immediately.
The haste is generated within the girl herself as she acts on her mother's instigation, an immediate self-driven urgency rather than bestowed or received from elsewhere.

This occurrence matches the term's usual 'haste/speed' sense (as also in Luke 1:39), showing no divergence from its typical usage; the surface form meta spoudes is the standard idiom for 'with haste.'
The immediate response shown is urgent resolve -- the girl moves at once to press her request without delay or hesitation.
No lasting inner quality or capacity is established by this single act of haste; it is a momentary manner of action in this scene.
No change in the girl's condition or disposition is shown; haste describes the manner of an already-decided action, not a transformation.
No before/during/after sequence of inner states is depicted; haste marks the manner of a single continuous action.
No mechanism producing change is shown; haste is the manner in which the already-formed demand is carried out.
Haste operates as the manner-mode of urgent, immediate action -- entering and asking without delay.
No specific constitutional level (spirit/soul/heart/mind/body part) is named for haste in this verse; it describes outward manner of action.
Haste here engages volition and agency -- it reflects the girl's determined, urgent will acting swiftly on her mother's instigation to press the demand.
Haste here is not movement toward God -- it describes urgent approach to a human king to demand an execution, not seeking, supplication, or worship of God.
Haste is the girl's own manner of action, not an act proceeding from God toward a human person.
Haste is extended in the girl's approach toward the king -- she brings her mother's demand to him with urgent immediacy, operating as the pressing manner of that interpersonal request.
Haste is not depicted as taken up by the girl from another party here; it is her own manner in carrying out the demand (following her mother's instigation, but the haste itself is her own action).
No relation to angelic or adversarial beings is shown.
Haste is not predicated of God here; it describes purely human urgency in the girl's approach to Herod to demand John's execution.
Asked (αἰτέω) names the girl's formal request to the king; its role/effect is to convert her mother's instigation into a direct, binding demand upon Herod.
The immediate response shown is decisive, urgent demand -- the girl moves straight to stating exactly what she wants, without hesitation.
No lasting inner state or capacity is produced by this single request; it is a momentary act within the narrative.
No change in the girl's own condition or disposition is shown; she acts to secure an external outcome from the king.
No before/during/after sequence of inner states is shown; the asking is a single decisive act.
No mechanism of inner change is shown; asking here is the immediate execution of the already-formed demand from want (M18).
Asking operates as a direct, spoken demand mode -- verbally stating exactly what is wanted to the one with power to grant it.
No specific constitutional level (spirit/soul/heart/mind/body part) is named for this asking in the verse.
The asking originates within the girl herself as she acts on the wish (M18) instigated by her mother -- self-generated in the moment, though the underlying motive was received from another.
Asking here engages volition and agency -- the girl exercises her will directly, actively demanding rather than merely wishing.
This asking is directed at a human king, not toward God; it is not an act of seeking, supplication, or worship of God.
Asking here is the girl's own act toward the king, not an act proceeding from God toward a human person.
Asking is extended by the girl toward the king -- it operates as a direct interpersonal demand pressed upon him for an immediate act (John's head).
Asking is not depicted as something the girl takes up from another; rather she carries her mother's instigated wish forward as her own request to the king.
No angelic or adversarial being is in view; the asking is directed at the human king Herod.
This asking is not predicated of God nor related to God; it is a purely human demand made to King Herod.
Want (θέλω) names the girl's stated desire; its role is to declare the specific outcome she is demanding -- John's head on a platter.
The immediate expression shown is a blunt, specific declaration of the desired outcome -- 'I want... at once' -- reflecting resolute will with no hesitation.
No lasting inner quality or capacity is produced by this single expressed want; it is a momentary declaration within the scene.
No change in the girl's own condition or disposition is shown; she expresses an already-fixed desire, not a transformation.
No before/during/after sequence of inner states is shown; want is voiced as a single fixed declaration.
The mechanism producing this want is the mother's instigation -- the desire was formed through another's influence and is here voiced by the girl as her own.
Want operates in the mode of direct volitional declaration -- stating the desired outcome plainly and pressing for its immediate fulfillment.
No specific constitutional level (spirit/soul/heart/mind/body part) is named for want in this verse.
The want is received from another person -- the girl's mother instigated the request, which the girl voices as her own desire to the king.
Want engages the volitional faculty directly -- it is the girl's own will expressed and pressed as demand upon the king.
This want is directed at a human king for a violent request, not movement toward God in seeking or worship.
Want here is the girl's own desire directed at the king, not an act proceeding from God toward a human person.
Want is extended by the girl toward the king as the content of her demand -- it operates as the interpersonal expression of what she requires of him.
The want the girl voices is taken up from her mother's instigation (implied by the wider narrative) -- she adopts and voices as her own the desire her mother directed her to express.
No angelic or adversarial being is involved; the want is directed at the human king Herod.
This want is not predicated of God nor related to God; it is a human desire voiced to a human king.
'In' (came in) is a plain movement-verb describing entrance, a supporting operation-word.
'Immediately' is a manner adverb intensifying the speed of the entrance; it modifies the operation rather than naming its own characteristic.
'With' is a preposition linking 'haste' to the action; it carries no independent characteristic.
'To' is a preposition marking direction toward the king; it names no characteristic of its own.
'King' names Herod's office/role; it is a supporting referential noun, not its own inner-being characteristic.
'Saying' introduces the girl's direct speech; it is a supporting speech-act verb, not its own characteristic.
'Give' is the plain operation-verb demanded of the king, a supporting act-word not its own characteristic.
'Me' is a plain first-person pronoun, the recipient of the demanded act; it names no characteristic of its own.
'Once' (at once) is a manner adverb intensifying the immediacy demanded; it qualifies the operation rather than naming its own characteristic.
'Head' names the literal body part demanded; it is a supporting concrete noun, not an inner-being characteristic.
'John' is a proper name identifying John the Baptist; it carries no meaningful inner-being sense to analyse.
'Baptist' is a title/epithet identifying John; it carries no independent inner-being characteristic to analyse here.
'On' is a preposition marking placement upon the platter; it carries no independent characteristic.
'Platter' names the literal serving dish demanded; it is a supporting concrete noun, not an inner-being characteristic.

As a genitive noun (N-GSF) inside the phrase 'with haste,' this occurrence's form shows spoude (haste) functioning as the manner of Herodias's daughter's entry, naming the urgency driving her approach to the king.
In the fixed phrase meta spoudes (with haste), this occurrence means literal physical speed/urgency of movement, the girl's rushing entrance to make her request, not zeal or diligence.

Here spoude marks the abruptness with which the request follows the mother's instruction, implying a constitutional urgency that colors the demand for John's head as impulsive rather than deliberated.
Rooted in speudo (to hasten), the term here operates as literal speed of physical movement into the king's presence, showing bodily urgency rather than inner earnestness.
As a genitive singular feminine noun governed by the preposition meta ('with'), the form functions adverbially, describing the manner of her coming in rather than naming an independent quality.

This occurrence sits at the 'haste/speed' end of the term's semantic range (as opposed to its 'zeal/earnestness' extension seen elsewhere, e.g. Rom.12.11), showing the physical rather than dispositional sense operating here.
This occurrence expresses an act (the manner of her hurried coming) rather than a settled disposition or received quality.
No related term functioning as this occurrence's structural opposite (e.g. a term for delay/sloth) is present in this verse's context.
No person-type term (one habitually characterized by haste) is relevant to or present in this occurrence.
No supplication/seeking term for obtaining haste from another applies to this occurrence.
As NT Greek narrative prose describing a court scene, the Testament context makes no special interpretive difference here beyond the ordinary Koine sense of hastening.
Spoude is attested in classical Greek (e.g. Herodotus, Thucydides) well before the NT period; this occurrence uses the term's established pre-NT sense of haste/speed, not a NT-period coinage.
The middle-voice aorist form (V-AMI-3S) shows the girl asking on her own behalf/for her own benefit, consistent with the middle sense of aiteo as claiming or requesting something for oneself.
Here aiteo means to ask/request of a superior (the king), functioning at the definitional level as a formal demand made to one with power to grant it.
The relational implication here is directional: the asking moves from an inferior party (the girl) to a superior (the king), carrying an expectation that he will grant it.
The root sense of aiteo, 'to ask/request,' operates here as a direct verbal petition put to the king for a specific object (the head on a platter).
As an aorist middle indicative verb, the form shows a completed, self-interested act of requesting, framing her question as a decisive single act rather than an ongoing plea.

This occurrence sits within the term's ordinary 'ask a person for a thing' range (accusative person + thing), not its logical/postulate or borrowing extensions, showing a straightforward request-of-a-superior sense.
This occurrence expresses an act (the specific act of requesting) rather than a disposition.
No related term functioning as a structural opposite (e.g. a term for refusing/withholding) is present in this occurrence's context.
No person-type term (one who habitually asks/petitions) is relevant to this occurrence.
Aiteo itself is the term's own supplication/seeking-from-another sense; here it directly names the act of the girl seeking the head from the king.
As NT Greek narrative describing a request to Herod, Testament context makes no special interpretive difference beyond ordinary Koine usage of asking a superior for something.
Aiteo is well attested in classical Greek from Homer onward; this occurrence uses its established pre-NT sense of asking/demanding, not a NT-period coinage.
This occurrence matches the term's usual 'ask/request of a superior' sense; no divergence from the ordinary usage is shown here.
The present active indicative first-person form (V-PAI-1S) shows the girl expressing her own immediate, ongoing will directly to the king, naming a present act of willing rather than a settled trait.
Here thelo means 'I wish/want,' functioning definitionally as a direct statement of personal desire preceding and driving the specific request that follows.

The implication here is constitutional: the girl asserts her own will as the driving force behind the demand, framing the request as an expression of what she herself wants rather than a mere relay of her mother's instruction.
The root sense of thelo, an act of will/wish, operates here as the stated motive introducing her specific demand ('I want you to give me... the head').

As a present active first-person singular verb followed by an infinitive/subjunctive construction, the form shows a direct, present-tense assertion of personal will governing the following clause of what should be given.

This occurrence sits within the term's core volitional range ('to will, wish, want'), specifically the sense of a firm intention/decision (cf. Lk 14:28) rather than mere inclination, matching her decisive framing of the demand.
This occurrence expresses an act of willing/wanting in the moment, rather than a fixed disposition.
No related term functioning as a structural opposite (e.g. a term for reluctance/refusal) is present in this occurrence's context.
No person-type term (one who habitually wills/desires) is relevant to this occurrence.

No separate supplication/seeking term is relevant here; the wanting itself is expressed directly by thelo, with the actual seeking-from-another carried by the neighboring verb aiteo, not by this term.
As NT Greek narrative dialogue, the Testament context makes no special interpretive difference here beyond ordinary Koine usage of thelo as 'want/wish.'
Thelo/ethelo is attested in classical Greek from Homer onward; this occurrence uses its established pre-NT sense of wishing/wanting, not a NT-period coinage.
This occurrence matches the term's usual 'wish/want' sense as a stated personal desire; no divergence from the ordinary usage is shown here.

observations.text: Meaning: here the fear before Jesus' act, or before a word about judgment, ends in asking him to go. Implies: set beside FE-127, the verses state two ends of fear before the holy: glorifying God, or "depart". The verse gives no reason for the Gerasenes beyond "great fear".

verses.text: But they did not understand this saying, and it was concealed from them, so that they might not perceive it. And they were afraid to ask him about this saying.

observations.text: Meaning: each time Jesus foretells his death, the verses set not understanding beside a fear that keeps them from asking. Implies: Luk 9:45 is already in 10.2. Mar 10:32 does not name what they feared (R). The death side of the sayings is held.
Inside one person, perception is blocked, then fear, then rivalry (Luk 9:45-46).

What it leads to, in the person. Fear to ask (Luk 9:45); a plea, "I am a sojourner on the earth; hide not your commandments from me!" (Psa 119:19); searching, "the glory of kings is to search things out" (Pro 25:2); obedience to what is revealed, "the things that are revealed belong to us … that we may do all the words of this law" (Deu 29:29). Job 3:23, "a man whose way is hidden, whom God has hedged in", is the not-knowing that hems in.

Seat.; In the verse: none of the 13 names a seat.; In the passage — new in v3: in six passages the seat arrives close by. Each time it is genuine, but it belongs to a different party or plays a different role: The other party names it. Luk 9:45–46 → 9:47 "But Jesus, knowing the reasoning of their hearts, took a child". The disciples' blocked perception, their fear of asking and their rivalry have no seat word. The seat appears only when Jesus reads it: their hearts, known by another. This matches what v1 §3 item 1 found for doubt (Luk 24:38): the seat is named when someone diagnoses.; The offender's heart as the cause. Isa 29:14 ← 29:13 "their hearts are far from me" (v2; Batch G v3 §12.3). Hidden discernment is the consequence of a heart that has gone elsewhere.; The bearer's own heart as the prayer's end. Psa 19:12 (hidden faults) → 19:14 "Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in your sight". The one who cannot see his own hidden faults hands the heart's meditation over to God's sight. What is hidden from the self is entrusted to the one from whom nothing is hidden (§6).; The bearer's own soul as the source of the plea. Psa 119:19 ("hide not your commandments from me!") → 119:20 "My soul is consumed with longing for your rules at all times". The plea not to have the commandments hidden comes from a soul consumed with longing for them. Here the not-knowing is feared, and the fear comes from desire, the reverse of Luk 9:45, where the disciples are afraid to ask.; Heart and soul in the response to what is revealed. Deu 29:29 → 30:2 "return to the Lord your God … and obey his voice … with all your heart and with all your soul". The revealed things (29:29) are to be done, and the next verses place that doing in the whole heart and soul.; The sufferer's soul. Job 3:23 ("a man whose way is hidden") sits in the passage opened by "life to the bitter in soul" (3:20; see §4). The hemmed-in man is the bitter soul.
Luk 9:45–47: perception blocked from outside → fear to ask → rivalry → Jesus knows the reasoning of their hearts (v3)

verses.text: And I tell you, ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.

observations.text: In Luke.11.9 zēteō is a direct imperative parallel to ask/knock, within its ordinary volitional-seeking sense; no divergence.

In Luke.11.9, zēteō (seek) co-occurs with M21 (ask); both are commanded parallel spiritual postures (ask/seek/knock) toward God, complementary rather than one modifying the other -- seeking adds the dimension of active pursuit alongside asking's dimension of verbal request.
In Luke.11.9, zēteō (seek) is role-T3, an imperative from Jesus to 'you' (disciples/hearers) directing them to seek, with the implicit divine addressee as the one from whom finding results.

verses.text: For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened.

observations.text: In Matt.7.7, Matt.7.8, and Luke.11.10, 'seek/seeks' sits squarely within the base gloss of active seeking/pursuing in the parallelism of ask-seek-knock; no distinctive nuance beyond ordinary usage.
In Matt.7.7, Matt.7.8, and Luke.11.10, no other M-code characteristic is tagged in the role list alongside G2212 -- it stands as the sole M-coded term in these verses.

In Matt.7.7/Matt.7.8/Luke.11.10, 'seek' is directed by the disciple/petitioner (party, 2nd person addressed) toward an unnamed sought object, paralleling 'ask' toward God and 'knock' toward a door -- the seeking party initiates, the implied divine giver receives the action's aim.

observations.text: In Luke.12.48 'required' translates G2212 in its demand/exact sense rather than the base 'look for/seek' gloss -- the divergence carries a legal-accountability nuance (a master requiring an accounting of what was entrusted), impacting the reading toward stewardship-judgment rather than simple search; this contrasts with the neutral-search sense in Matt.7.7-8/Luke.11.10.
In Luke.12.48, no other M-code characteristic co-occurs with G2212 'required' in the given role list; it stands alone as the home-cluster term establishing this verse's relational chain.

In Luke.12.48, 'required' (G2212) is initiated by an unnamed authority/master (implied party) directed toward 'him' (the entrusted party) to whom much was given -- the operation runs from giver-turned-judge toward recipient-turned-accountable-party.

Knowing it.: *"If anyone's will is to do God's will, he will know whether the teaching is from God"* (Joh 7:17). The willing comes first, and the knowing follows it.; Paul was *"appointed … to know his will"* (Act 22:14), and was told the next moment *"why do you wait?"* (22:16).; *"Do not be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is"* (Eph 5:17), with *"be filled with the Spirit"* (5:18).; Knowing can stand without doing: *"you … know his will and approve what is excellent"* (Rom 2:18), said to one who *"boast[s] in God"* (2:17) and teaches others (2:19–21).; The servant *"who knew his master's will but did not get ready or act according to his will"* is beaten more than the one who did not know (Luk 12:47–48).

observations.text: In John.16.19 zeteo shifts toward the sense 'inquire/discuss/question among yourselves' (the disciples questioning each other about the meaning of Jesus's saying), aligning with the tree's documented sense 'to inquire or ask questions' rather than physical search -- a cognitive/interpretive nuance distinct from the searching-for-a-person sense used elsewhere in John.

M15 (knew/ginosko, Jesus's knowledge) and M18 (wanted/thelo, the disciples' desire) co-occur with M83 seeking in John.16.19: Jesus's perceptive knowledge (M15) discerns the disciples' desire (M18) to ask, which surfaces as their mutual questioning (M83/zeteo). The seeking here is the visible symptom of the underlying want that Jesus's knowledge already perceives -- an epistemic chain (knowledge -> desire -> inquiry) rather than seeking acting on the others.

In John.16.19 the seeking/inquiring operation is initiated by the disciples (party, T8 via Jesus's interlocutors) directed toward one another ('among yourselves') and ultimately toward understanding Jesus's own saying.
In John.16.19 erotao is used in its plain interrogative sense 'to ask/question' Jesus about the meaning of his saying -- sitting within the base gloss with no notable divergence.

verses.text: After these things Joseph of Arimathea, who was a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews, asked Pilate that he might take away the body of Jesus, and Pilate gave him permission. So he came and took away his body.

observations.text: Meaning: fear of people stops speech (Joh 7:13), keeps a disciple secret (Joh 19:38), locks a door (Joh 20:19), and draws a man back from the table (Gal 2:12). Joh 9:22 states what was feared: being put out of the synagogue. Implies: Gal 2:13 names what followed as hypocrisy. At the locked door, the answer is a presence and a word ("Peace be with you"), and then "the disciples were glad when they saw the Lord" (Joh 20:20).

Fear leads to hiding, distance: "I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself"; "the people were afraid and trembled, and they stood far off"; "secretly for fear of the Jews"; "the doors being locked … for fear of the Jews"
Fear and Doubt and hiding (M20): Fear and hiding; "O you of little faith, why did you doubt?"; a secret disciple (verses shared or near: 16 / 8).

Hiding from people: Much of the hiding in Scripture is from people who could do harm, and in these verses it is the weaker side that hides. "When the wicked rise, people hide themselves" (Proverbs 28:28). "The poor of the earth all hide themselves" (Job 24:4). When Israel hid in the caves, "all the people followed him trembling" (1 Samuel 13:7).; Often the verse records not the feeling of the one who hides but someone else's counsel to hide.; Jonathan: "Saul my father seeks to kill you … Stay in a secret place and hide yourself" (1 Samuel 19:2).; God to Elijah: "hide yourself by the brook Cherith" (1 Kings 17:3).; Where the feeling is named, it is fear.; Jacob fled from Laban "secretly", and he said why: "Because I was afraid" (Genesis 31:27, 31).; Joseph of Arimathea was "a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews". The same verse ends with him going to Pilate and taking away the body (John 19:38).; Hiding can be good sense: "The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it" (Proverbs 22:3). It ends when the news changes. The men who had hidden in the hills "heard that the Philistines were fleeing, they too followed hard after them in the battle" (1 Samuel 14:22).; And sometimes hiding is refused, or impossible.; The servant chooses not to hide: "I gave my back to those who strike … I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting" (Isaiah 50:6).; No one can hide from a friend who turns: "it is not an adversary who deals insolently with me — then I could hide from him. But it is you, a man, my equal, my companion, my familiar friend" (Psalm 55:12–13).

Where inner being is present, it sits behind the act (phenomenon.set hidden-behind-act), and the motive is named by *another cluster's* word: fear: Gen 3:10 ("I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself"); Mat 25:25 ("I was afraid, and I went and hid your talent"); Joh 19:38 ("secretly for fear of the Jews"); Dan 10:7 ("a great trembling fell upon them, and they fled to hide themselves"); 1Ch 21:20 (Ornan's sons hid on seeing the angel); shame or withdrawal: Luk 1:24, Elizabeth "kept herself hidden". The motive follows in 1:25: "to take away my reproach among people".; Hiding is the body's answer to fear. The seat is replaced by the act together with the fear word.
How it co-exists across the strands. Trembling (1Sa 13:7; Dan 10:7), fear (Gen 31:31; Joh 19:38), and seeing danger (Pro 22:3; 1Ch 21:20). Its opposite is the prudent/simple pair (f).

verses.text: You desire and do not have, so you murder. You covet and cannot obtain, so you fight and quarrel. You do not have, because you do not ask.

observations.text: Factor Joined with: Confirmed. grief (Mar 3:5); jealousy, which makes it unappeasable (Pro 6:34; 27:4); envy (Gal 5:26; Jam 4:2); the Spirit (1Sa 11:6).
Sequence in Jam 4:1–3: passions at war within → desire unmet → murder, covet → fight and quarrel → not asking → asking wrongly.

Anger and Desire, jealousy, envy (M18): Jealousy named with God's anger; "jealousy makes a man furious"; "the anger and envy that you showed because of your hatred"; "You covet and cannot obtain, so you fight and quarrel".

passions at war within → quarrels and fights (Jam 4:1); covet, cannot obtain → fight and quarrel (4:2); jealousy and strife → of the flesh (1Cor 3:3); conceit, craving → quarrels about words → envy, dissension, slander (1Ti 6:4); controversies → breed quarrels (2Ti 2:23).

Where it comes from. Every verse, or the one next to it, names a source, and the sources are inner: Passions at war within: "What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you? You desire and do not have, so you murder. You covet and cannot obtain, so you fight and quarrel" (Jam 4:1–2). The outer fight is the inner war carried outward; The flesh: "for you are still of the flesh. For while there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not of the flesh and behaving only in a human way?" (1Cor 3:3), after "I could not address you as spiritual people, but as people of the flesh" (3:1); Conceit: "Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another" (Gal 5:26). "He is puffed up with conceit and understands nothing. He has an unhealthy craving for controversy" (1Ti 6:4); Appetite: the dividers "do not serve our Lord Christ, but their own appetites [belly]" (Rom 16:18); Envy and selfish ambition behind a good act: "Some indeed preach Christ from envy and rivalry, but others from good will … The former proclaim Christ out of selfish ambition, not sincerely but thinking to afflict me" (Phili 1:15–17). The same outward act, preaching, has opposite inner sources; A depraved mind: "constant friction among people who are depraved in mind and deprived of the truth, imagining that godliness is a means of gain" (1Ti 6:5); Controversies themselves: "foolish, ignorant controversies … breed quarrels" (2Ti 2:23); "avoid foolish controversies, genealogies, dissensions, and quarrels about the law" (Tit 3:9).

How it co-exists: With envy, often (5 of the 11 verses). Envy is paired with strife in Gal 5:26; Phili 1:15; 1Ti 6:4; 1Cor 3:3 ("jealousy"); in Jam 4:2 it is "covet"; With its named opposites: "that there be no divisions among you, but that you be united in the same mind and the same judgment" (1Cor 1:10); "godliness with contentment is great gain" (1Ti 6:6); "the Lord's servant must not be quarrelsome but kind to everyone … correcting his opponents with gentleness" (2Ti 2:24–25); "keep in step with the Spirit" (Gal 5:25).

What it leads to. Separation from the divider: "avoid them" (Rom 16:17); "after warning him once and then twice, have nothing more to do with him … he is self-condemned" (Tit 3:10–11). "You do not have, because you do not ask" (Jam 4:2), so strife blocks asking.
(v2) Jam 4:1–3: Sequence the text gives: passions at war within → desire unmet → murder, covet → fight and quarrel → not asking → asking wrongly.

Jam 4:10: "Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you.": This is the end of a run of commands that begins at 4:6, "God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble". The commands are: "Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil … Draw near to God … Cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded. Be wretched and mourn and weep. Let your laughter be turned to mourning" (4:7–9); In this passage, humbling oneself is not one act but the whole movement the verses list: submitting, resisting, drawing near, cleansing, purifying the heart, mourning. "Before the Lord" names who it faces; The passage opens with the quarrels that come from "your passions … at war within you" (4:1). Jam 4:1–8 are cited across 10.6, 10.7, 10.13, Ch 11, 12 and 13.1. 4:10 is not.

Passage: *"your passions are at war within you … You desire and do not have, so you murder. You covet and cannot obtain, so you fight and quarrel. You do not have, because you do not ask"* (4:1–2). Then 4:4: *"friendship with the world is enmity with God."*

Toward the world: *"whoever wishes to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God"* (Jam 4:4). The verses before: *"your passions are at war within you … You desire and do not have, so you murder"* (4:1–2).

verses.text: but in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect,

observations.text: Meaning: toward people, the ESV renders phobos (fear) as "respect". It is shown to the unjust as well as the good (1Pe 2:18) and goes with the hope of winning others (3:1–2). R: in 1Pe 3:15 the verse does not say whether the "respect" is toward the one who asks or toward God. I read it as open.

Meaning: in 1Pe 3:14–15 the same root is forbidden (fear of those who make you suffer) and asked for (the "respect" of the answer). The verse puts honouring Christ "in your hearts" between them. Implies: this is the clearest case in the unit of the word changing character within one sentence. (Counted against this unit only; Rom 13:3–7 is the other.)
Forbidden and asked for, close together: "Have no fear of them" … "with gentleness and respect"; "do not fear what they fear" … "Let him be your fear"

Face E. Awe, respect or reverence toward people (7 / 6 hits and verses; surfaces respect · respectful · respects · feared): The fear root rendered "respect": to rulers, masters, husbands, any who ask; Herod toward John.
Forbidden and asked for, two verses apart: "Have no fear of them" … "with gentleness and respect".
The Greek fear words G5401 and G5399 is rendered respect: Rom 13:7, 1Pe 2:18, 3:15.

In meeting someone who is wrong or opposed: "restore him in a spirit of gentleness. Keep watch on yourself, lest you too be tempted" (Gal 6:1). The verse joins the gentle restoring to watching oneself. Two verses on: "if anyone thinks he is something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself" (6:3); "correcting his opponents with gentleness. God may perhaps grant them repentance" (2Ti 2:25). The correcting is gentle, and the outcome is left to God; "make a defense … yet do it with gentleness and respect" (1Pe 3:15); "Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love in a spirit of gentleness?" (1Cor 4:21). Said to those who "are arrogant" (4:18); "to be gentle, and to show perfect courtesy toward all people. For we ourselves were once foolish" (Tit 3:2–3). The ground of the gentleness is the memory of what "we ourselves" were.

Already cited: Jam 1:21 in Ch 14; Phili 2:8 in Ch 2; 1Pe 3:15 in 10.12; Jam 4:6 in Ch 11 and 13.1; 2Cor 7:6 in 10.6; 1Pe 3:4 in Ch 1 and Ch 9; Col 3:12 in 10.7 and Ch 11; 1Cor 4:21 in 10.10 and 10.7; Phili 3:21 in Ch 2; 2Ti 2:25 in 13.3; 1Pe 5:5 and Tit 3:2 in 10.10; Mat 11:29 in Ch 11; Jam 3:13 in 10.6.

7.2 Holiness of the human inner seat: "may your whole spirit and soul and body be kept blameless" — "the God of peace himself sanctify you completely" (1Th 5:23) [H1] — the one verse naming spirit, soul and body together; "cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and spirit, bringing holiness to completion" (2Co 7:1) [H2]; "how to be holy in body and spirit" (1Co 7:34) [H2]; "establish your hearts blameless in holiness" (1Th 3:13); "in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy" (1Pe 3:15); "the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit" (1Pe 3:4) [H1]

10. Gentleness — the spirit as the manner of approach: "What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love in a spirit of gentleness?" (1Co 4:21) [X]; "you who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness. Keep watch on yourself" (Gal 6:1) [X]; "the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit" (1Pe 3:4) [H1]; "I am gentle and lowly in heart" (Mat 11:29); "receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls" (Jam 1:21); "make a defense … with gentleness and respect, having a good conscience" (1Pe 3:15–16); [Claude reading] "Spirit" here names the manner in which one person comes to another (1Co 4:21; Gal 6:1) — the disposition [X] governing an encounter. Where gentleness is located in the heart (Mat 11:29), it is a settled character. Where it is "of spirit", it is the bearing brought to a specific meeting.

6.4 Hope and the NT inner seat: "my heart was glad … my flesh also will dwell in hope" (Act 2:26) — flesh in hope; "hope does not put us to shame, because God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit" (Rom 5:5) [D1]; "by the power of the Holy Spirit you may abound in hope" (Rom 15:13) [D1]; "through the Spirit, by faith, we ourselves eagerly wait for the hope of righteousness" (Gal 5:5) [D3]; "one body and one Spirit … one hope" (Eph 4:4) [D1]; "the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope" (Eph 1:18); "in your hearts honor Christ … a reason for the hope that is in you" (1Pe 3:15); "waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him" (Luk 2:25) [D1]

observations.text: Praying it.: *"Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven"* (Mat 6:10). It is the prayer taught, before bread and forgiveness (6:11–12).; At Gethsemane, the second time: *"My Father, if this cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done"* (26:42). It comes after *"The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak"* (26:41). The words he taught are the words he prays.; Asking within it: *"if we ask anything according to his will he hears us"* (1Jo 5:14). The other side: *"If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you"* (Joh 15:7). The second verse leaves the wish open, but only for one in whom his words abide.; I read the two together. The asking is free where the asker's will has been shaped by his words.

The crossref v3 parser fails on that form. These references were written as "Jude 1:6" etc. for the narrative check only; the hits CSV keeps the DB form.

Romans 11:7: "Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened": Paul asks whether God has rejected his people and answers: *"By no means!"* (v1). *"God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew"* (v2). He gives Elijah, who thought he was alone, and God's reply: *"I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal"* (v4). *"So too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace. But if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works"* (v5–6).; Then v7: *"What then? Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened"*.; The others are *"the rest"*. Two things are said of them: They were seeking (*epizēteō*, G1934) and did not obtain.; They were hardened (*pōroō*, G4456).; The hardening is described from Scripture: *"God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear, down to this very day"* (v8). The giving is God's act (rule 72, A). The eyes that do not see and ears that do not hear are in the human inner being.; Paul does not leave it there: *"So I ask, did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means! Rather, through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles, so as to make Israel jealous"* (v11). He goes on: *"how much more will their full inclusion mean!"* (v12).

What this verse shows of others around the choosing: Those who are not among the chosen are described as seeking and not obtaining.; They were hardened: eyes that do not see, ears that do not hear (v8).; The hardening is not the end. Their stumbling is not *"in order that they might fall"* (v11).; Jealousy is named as an aim: *"so as to make Israel jealous"* (v11).; The remnant is chosen *"by grace"*, not by works (v5–6). The verse says how the elect were chosen. It does not say why the rest were not.

1 Thessalonians 1:4: "For we know, brothers loved by God, that he has chosen you": Paul writes of what he remembers of them: *"your work of faith and labor of love and steadfastness of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ"* (v3). Then: *"For we know, brothers loved by God, that he has chosen you, because our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit and with full conviction"* (v4–5).; "Know" is *oida* (G6063). Here another person knows that someone has been chosen. The ESV joins v4 to v5 with "because": the knowing rests on how the gospel came to them. The passage goes on to what was seen in them: *"you received the word in much affliction, with the joy of the Holy Spirit"* (v6); *"you became an example to all the believers"* (v7); *"your faith in God has gone forth everywhere"* (v8); *"you turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God, and to wait for his Son from heaven"* (v9–10)
